prompt.context: This is a market sizing / estimation question. No additional background is provided beyond the question itself.
prompt.question: How many gas stations are there in the U.S.?

framework: Choose a segmentation approach: population-based or demand-based
Population-based: segment by area type (urban, suburban, rural) and estimate people-per-station in each, then aggregate to national level
Demand-based: estimate total gallons consumed nationally, estimate gallons sold per station per year, then divide
Sanity-check both approaches against each other and against intuition (1,000 is too few; 1,000,000 is too many)
Show transparent reasoning; prioritize logical structure over arithmetic precision

questions.prompt: Approach 1 (Population): Estimate the number of gas stations using population density segmentation
questions.guidance: Anchor on a known locale. Example: Menlo Park/Atherton has ~15 stations for ~40,000 people (~1 per 2,667 people). Urban areas are less dense in stations (e.g., SF: ~150 stations for 700,000 people). Rural areas are more dense in stations (e.g., 3 stations for 5,000 people). A reasonable national blended ratio is ~1 station per 2,667 people. Apply to U.S. population of 250 million to arrive at ~90,000 stations.

math.setup: National stations = U.S. population / people-per-station ratio
steps: Anchor ratio: 15 stations / 40,000 people = 1 station per 2,667 people

questions.prompt: Approach 2 (Demand): Estimate the number of gas stations using gasoline consumption data
questions.guidance: Estimate total U.S. gasoline demand, then divide by per-station supply capacity. Key assumptions: 125 million cars on the road, each driven 12,000 miles/year at 20 mpg = 75 billion gallons/year total demand. Average station: 8 pumps, 4 in use on average, 14 hours open per day, 6 fills/hour per pump, 10 gallons per fill = 3,360 gallons/day = ~1.2 million gallons/year per station. Dividing gives ~62,500 stations.

math.setup: Stations = Total annual U.S. gasoline consumption / Annual gallons sold per station
steps: Total demand: 125M cars × 12,000 miles ÷ 20 mpg = 75,000,000,000 gallons/year
Gallons per station per day: 4 pumps × 6 fills/hr × 10 gal/fill × 14 hr = 3,360 gal/day
Gallons per station per year: 3,360 × 365 ≈ 1,226,400 ≈ 1.2M gal/year

questions.prompt: Reconcile both approaches and state a final estimate
questions.guidance: Both approaches land in the 60,000–90,000 range, which is consistent. The actual figure at time of the case was approximately 80,000 stations. Acknowledge that the goal is transparent, logical reasoning, not a precisely correct number. Note that simple, easy-to-compute numbers are preferred under interview conditions.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors could cause your estimate to be too high or too low?

categories.name: Too High
ideas: Urban stations handle far more volume per pump than suburban/rural stations
Multi-pump highway truck stops inflate gallons-per-station above average
Growing EV adoption reduces gasoline demand

categories.name: Too Low
ideas: Truck stops and commercial fueling depots not captured in the passenger car model
Rural stations with very low volume still exist due to service needs
Combination convenience stores may count as stations even if fuel is secondary

categories.name: Simplification Assumptions to Flag
ideas: Averaging people-per-station across area types introduces estimation error
Using 20 mpg ignores the mix of trucks, SUVs, and fuel-efficient cars
Station open hours and pump utilization vary significantly by location

recommendation: Final estimate: approximately 75,000–90,000 gas stations in the U.S.
Both population-based (~90,000) and demand-based (~62,500) approaches converge in the same order of magnitude, supporting confidence in the range
risks: Shift toward electric vehicles could make the estimate outdated quickly
High variance in station throughput across urban vs. rural locations makes a single average unreliable
next_steps: Refine the demand-based model by segmenting vehicles (passenger cars vs. trucks/commercial)
Cross-check against industry data sources (e.g., U.S. Energy Information Administration)
